title: Uttar Pradesh Intensifies Crackdown on Adulterated Paneer, Khoya, and Milk
excerpt: UP's Food Safety Department has collected ₹55 crore in fines over 11 months as part of a year-round enforcement drive targeting fake dairy products, with the state acting under FSSAI's nationwide directive against adulteration in milk, paneer, and khoya.
body:
• Uttar Pradesh's Food Safety and Drug Administration (FSDA) has collected approximately ₹55.34 crore in fines from April 2025 to February 2026, conducting over 1.76 lakh inspections targeting food adulteration.
  • The state is operating under CM Yogi Adityanath's 'Zero Tolerance' policy, with dedicated teams inspecting dairy production units and publicly displaying photographs of identified adulterators.
  • FSSAI has issued a nationwide directive under Section 16(5) of the Food Safety Act, mandating all states to launch special enforcement drives against adulteration in milk, paneer, and khoya.
  • The crackdown follows Maharashtra's statewide ban on fake paneer and aligns with growing national concern over synthetic dairy products found to contain urea, detergent, and palm oil.

Uttar Pradesh is escalating its war on food adulteration. The state's Food Safety and Drug Administration (FSDA) has moved from seasonal festival-time raids to a continuous, year-round enforcement operation targeting adulterated dairy products — particularly paneer, khoya, and milk — that are manufactured and distributed across the state's vast food supply chain.

₹55 Crore in Fines, 1.76 Lakh Inspections

Between April 2025 and February 2026, UP's FSDA conducted over 1.76 lakh surveys and raids, collecting approximately ₹55.34 crore in fines from food adulteration cases. The scale of enforcement is unprecedented for the state.

"Earlier in UP, campaigns against adulteration used to be limited to festivals. Now they are being run throughout the year. The department has been given a free hand to take action when irregularities are found."

— Dayashankar Mishra, UP Minister of State for Food Safety

The problem is deeply entrenched. In a single raid in Meerut's Nagla Kumbha village in April 2026, authorities seized 28 quintals of adulterated paneer, over 5,000 litres of fake milk, 1,100 litres of palm oil, and chemicals. The fake paneer — made from vegetable oil, flour, acetic acid, and urea with no actual milk content — was being supplied to Delhi-NCR and Uttarakhand. Two FIRs were registered in that case alone.

The Nationwide FSSAI Directive

UP's crackdown operates within a broader national framework. In December 2025, the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) issued a formal directive under Section 16(5) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, ordering all states and Union Territories to launch special enforcement drives against adulteration and misbranding of milk, paneer, and khoya.

The FSSAI directive mandates intensive inspections of both licensed and unlicensed dairy units, sample collection for laboratory testing, supply chain tracing, and strict enforcement including licence cancellation, seizure of unsafe products, and closure of illegal operations. States have been instructed to report enforcement actions in real-time through the Food Safety Compliance System (FoSCoS) and submit fortnightly reports.

Western UP: The Adulteration Stronghold

FSDA data reveals a clear geography of adulteration within UP. Western districts — Bareilly, Moradabad, Meerut, Agra, and Aligarh — are the primary hotspots for milk and dairy product adulteration. Kanpur and Agra lead in spice adulteration. The concentration in western UP is significant because these districts feed supply chains into Delhi-NCR, one of India's largest consumer markets.

CM Yogi Adityanath has directed officials to publicly display photographs of identified adulterators at major intersections — a measure designed to create social stigma alongside legal consequences. The state has also expanded its network of food and drug testing laboratories, with new facilities operational in Aligarh, Ayodhya, and Kanpur, and upgraded microbiology labs in Lucknow, Meerut, and Varanasi.

Part of a Broader National Trend

UP's intensified enforcement follows similar action in other states. Maharashtra recently imposed a statewide ban on fake paneer, and FSSAI has cracked down on misleading food labels nationwide. The pattern reflects growing consumer awareness and political pressure around food safety — particularly for dairy staples like paneer, khoya, and ghee that form the backbone of Indian cooking.

For the Indian diaspora, the adulteration issue carries personal weight. Many NRIs source ghee, paneer, and mithai from India for personal consumption or gifts, and concerns about product authenticity have driven demand for certified organic and traceable dairy brands both domestically and in export markets.
